strengths: Technically sound and well-motivated: the diagnostic experiment (Figure 2c) convincingly shows that GCRL policies degrade with goal distance even though their value functions encode useful reachability geometry, which grounds the central claim that long-horizon failures come from failing to exploit this geometry.

Simple, practical method: TTGS is training-free, adds only test-time computation (graph construction ~45-100s, ~0.8s per-episode path computation, ~1ms per step), and plugs into existing value-based GCRL agents without modifying training. This is an attractive and easily adoptable contribution.

Strong empirical gains on OGBench giant mazes (e.g., HIQL 0.0→80.9 on pointmaze-giant-stitch, GCIQL 0.0→98.0, HIQL 4.4→78.1 on humanoidmaze-giant-stitch), with 8 seeds, 50 rollouts per task, and mean±std reported following the benchmark protocol.

Useful ablations and sensitivity analyses: adaptive subgoal selection and the edge-length penalty are each validated (Figure 4a), sensitivity to τ and T is honestly reported (Table 2 shows large variance), and an alternative vertex-sampling scheme is described even though it did not help (Appendix C).

Fair treatment of baselines: the paper explicitly acknowledges that TTGS operates in a more constrained setting than GAS and CompDiffuser, reran GAS's official implementation over 8 seeds for all domains, and notes where GAS substantially outperforms TTGS (antmaze, visual tasks) rather than cherry-picking.
Honest limitations section covering computational overhead, dependence on base learner competence and distance accuracy, and possible suboptimal subgoal selection under limited coverage.
weaknesses: Limited originality: graph/landmark search over dataset states with value-derived distances is closely related to Eysenbach et al. (2019) (Search on the Replay Buffer), Savinov et al. (2018), Emmons et al. (2020), Zhu et al. (2023), and Baek et al. (2025). The delta over these works — using the base learner's own goal-conditioned value function as the edge cost and doing no training at all — is real but modest, and the paper could more sharply quantify what is new relative to Search on the Replay Buffer.

Hyperparameter selection is a significant confound: Table 4 shows per-dataset, per-agent values of τ and T (e.g., τ∈{6,12,24,36}), yet Table 2 shows results vary from 78.6±13.4 to 1.1±1.5 on antmaze-giant-stitch across settings. Since TTGS is evaluated on the same tasks used to choose these values, reported gains may be optimistic, and the claim that 'choosing hyperparameters is simple' is not well supported by the reported variance. A validation protocol (e.g., tuning on navigate and evaluating on stitch) is missing.

Results are inconsistent across base learners and environments: TTGS sometimes fails to help or gives near-zero gains (GCIQL/QRL on humanoidmaze-giant, all agents on visual-humanoidmaze, antmaze-giant-navigate GCIQL 0.4→5.4), and GAS substantially outperforms TTGS on antmaze and most visual tasks. The main results emphasis (Figure 3) on the tasks where TTGS shines somewhat overstates generality.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only OGBench locomotion/maze domains. Maze navigation is precisely the setting where Euclidean-like distances and graph search work best; evidence on manipulation tasks (e.g., OGBench kitchen/scene) or settings where state-space geometry is less informative is needed to support the 'broad applicability' claim.

QRL is included as a base learner, yet QRL's value is itself designed as a quasi-metric for planning (Wang et al., 2023), making the 'TTGS reveals unused geometric structure' framing partially circular for that agent; the distinction is not discussed.

Presentation issues: the code URL is a blank placeholder ('Our code is available at .'), and the Website field on page 1 is empty, undermining the reproducibility claim at submission time; comparisons partly rely on numbers copied from other papers (CompDiffuser) and a GAS re-run using antmaze hyperparameters on other domains, both acknowledged but still imperfect baselines.

No theoretical grounding for the soft-horizon penalty design (the superlinear penalty p(x)=x·1000^{x/τ} is ad hoc, and no analysis is given of when shortest paths over d̂ correspond to dynamically feasible plans).

strengths: Simple, practical, training-free method: TTGS requires no retraining, no extra supervision, and no online interaction, making it easy to adopt on top of existing value-based GCRL agents; the value-to-distance calibration (closed-form mappings for common reward conventions in Section 3.1) is a nice touch that makes the framework policy-agnostic.

Large and well-documented gains on the hardest OGBench long-horizon tasks (e.g., HIQL 0.0% to 80.9% on pointmaze-giant-stitch, HIQL 4.4% to 78.1% on humanoidmaze-giant-stitch), with results across three base learners (HIQL, GCIQL, QRL), three dataset regimes (stitch/navigate/explore), and pixel-based variants.

Reasonably thorough empirical apparatus: ablations of the subgoal-selection rule and edge penalty, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Table 2), an honest limitations section covering compute overhead and dependence on base-learner quality, and comparisons to concurrent planning baselines (GAS, CompDiffuser) with reproduction caveats clearly stated.
The framing that value functions already encode exploitable geometric structure that frozen policies fail to use at inference time is a useful, actionable insight for the offline GCRL community.
weaknesses: Limited originality: building a graph over dataset states and running shortest-path search to produce subgoals is a well-established idea (Savinov et al., 2018; Eysenbach et al., 2019; Emmons et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2023; concurrent Baek et al., 2025). The incremental contributions — the soft-horizon edge penalty, adaptive subgoal selection, and closed-form value-to-distance mappings — do not rise to the level of a new method or new understanding for a main-track paper.

The 'consistently improves or preserves' claim is overstated by the paper's own Table 3: GCIQL+TTGS shows no gain on humanoidmaze-giant-stitch (0.2% to 0.2%), degrades on several visual tasks (visual-antmaze-giant-navigate 0.5% to 0.2%; visual-antmaze-large-stitch 0.1% to 0.0%), and QRL+TTGS is flat or worse on multiple datasets. A more careful analysis of when and why TTGS fails is missing.

Comparison against the strongest planning baseline is unflattering and the narrative cherry-picks: on antmaze tasks GAS substantially outperforms TTGS (e.g., antmaze-large-explore 91.0 vs 26.6, antmaze-giant-stitch 86.2 vs 78.6, all visual-antmaze tasks by large margins), yet the abstract and introduction emphasize only cases where TTGS surpasses complex methods.

Potential test-set hyperparameter selection: τ and T are tuned per (dataset, base agent) pair (Table 4), which risks inflating TTGS results relative to base learners evaluated with default settings. The authors say sweeps were not extensive, but the protocol for selecting these values on evaluation environments is not described, raising a fairness concern.

Several reported results have very high variance (e.g., HIQL+TTGS on antmaze-large-explore: 26.6 ± 34.0), which weakens confidence in the claimed improvements; only visual and qualitative inspection (Figure 2, 4b) supports the motivational 'value functions encode geometry' claim rather than a quantitative analysis.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only OGBench maze/locomotion navigation; no manipulation, no real-robot, and no truly high-dimensional continuous-control results beyond humanoidmaze, which limits the claimed 'broad applicability'. The code link in the manuscript is blank, hurting reproducibility despite detailed appendices.

strengths: Simple, well-motivated, and practical method: TTGS is a training-free, inference-time planning wrapper that only requires a distance signal and the offline dataset, making it easy to adopt on top of existing value-based GCRL agents.

Strong and often dramatic empirical gains on the hardest OGBench tasks (e.g., HIQL 0.0% -> 80.9% on pointmaze-giant-stitch, HIQL 4.4% -> 78.1% on humanoidmaze-giant-stitch), demonstrating that frozen policies fail to exploit the geometry encoded in their own value functions.

Broad evaluation: three base learners (HIQL, GCIQL, QRL), state-based and visual variants, multiple data-collection regimes (stitch, navigate, explore), 8 seeds with 50 rollouts per task, plus ablations on subgoal selection, edge penalty, and sensitivity to tau/T.

Honest treatment of setting differences: the comparison to GAS and CompDiffuser in Appendix A clearly acknowledges that TTGS operates in a more constrained setting (no extra training), and the limitations section candidly discusses dependence on base-learner competence, distance accuracy, and dataset coverage.

Useful empirical insight: the value-to-step-distance calibration (closed forms for common reward conventions) is a clean, reusable contribution, and the finding that explicit search beats HIQL's learned high-level controller on giant mazes is interesting.

Reproducibility support is reasonable: full hyperparameter tables (Table 4), distance mappings per agent (Appendix B), computational cost measurements, and code availability (though the link is blank in the submitted PDF).
weaknesses: Limited originality: graph search over dataset states with value-derived distances is a well-trodden direction (Search on the Replay Buffer, Sparse Graphical Memory, Value Memory Graph, SPT/Siamese proximity predictors, GAS). The claimed differentiator—'no training, treats policies as black boxes'—is incremental; the method is largely a careful engineering assembly of known components.

The headline claim that TTGS 'consistently improves or preserves performance' is overstated. Table 3 contains degradations (e.g., GCIQL+TTGS on visual-antmaze-large-stitch, HIQL+TTGS on visual-humanoidmaze-medium-navigate 0.8 -> 0.4, QRL+TTGS visual-antmaze-large-navigate 0.9 -> 0.3) and many cases where TTGS remains near zero (GCIQL/QRL on humanoidmaze-giant-stitch). The claim of 'no statistically significant degradations' is asserted without a formal statistical test.

Potential evaluation leakage from hyperparameter tuning: tau is tuned per dataset/agent pair (tau ranges from 6 to 36 in Table 4), and the paper does not explain how tau and T were selected. If these were chosen on the evaluation tasks, the reported gains may be optimistic; a validation protocol or selection on held-out goals should be described.

Against trained planning baselines, TTGS is clearly weaker on the antmaze family (GAS: 76.0 vs. TTGS 65.8 on giant-navigate; 86.2 vs. 78.6 on giant-stitch; 91.0 vs. 26.6 on large-explore). The 'sometimes surpasses more complex methods' framing relies mostly on pointmaze and humanoidmaze results, and the abstract/intro could mislead readers about the overall comparison.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only OGBench locomotion/maze domains. Maze structure (walls, well-defined geometry) is arguably favorable to graph search; no manipulation or kitchen tasks, and no evidence the approach transfers beyond grid-like navigation.

Several results have very large variance (e.g., 26.6 ± 34.0 on antmaze-large-explore, 63.0 ± 28.1 visual-antmaze-medium-explore), making the reliability of the improvement estimates questionable in some settings.

The framework-level claim that any distance signal works is supported by only one alternative (body-position Euclidean distance), which is itself maze-adapted; the flexibility of the framework is therefore demonstrated only thinly.

Presentation issues: the code URL in Section 1 is blank in the submitted PDF; the website field on page 1 is empty; Figure 3 aggregates results without per-dataset numbers in the main text, requiring a trip to the appendix.

strengths: Technically solid and well-executed: the method is simple (graph over sampled dataset states, value-derived edge weights, Dijkstra, adaptive subgoal selection) and the paper is unusually thorough in supporting it with ablations — soft vs. hard penalty (Table 10, showing hard thresholding disconnects stitching graphs with disconnect ratios up to 0.99), adaptive vs. next-subgoal selection, threshold sweeps (Table 3), vertex-count scaling (Table 12), clustering vs. random sampling (Table 9), replanning (Table 13), and an L2-kNN landmark baseline (Table 7).

Strong empirical gains under strict constraints: on the hardest giant-stitch tasks TTGS lifts success from near zero to 80–98% (e.g., HIQL on pointmaze-giant-stitch 0.0→80.9%, GCIQL on humanoidmaze-giant-stitch 0.2→78.1%) with no training, no online interaction, and <1s planning overhead, and Table 4 shows broad improvements across five base learners including strong recent methods (SAW, OTA).

Honest and informative treatment of when the method fails: the paper clearly identifies that gains require intermediate dataset coverage, local policy reliability, and long-horizon stitching need; manipulation tasks are shown to fail for a principled reason (Figure 5, hop-ratio analysis), and a rollout-free hop-ratio diagnostic is proposed and validated (Table 8), which is a useful practical contribution beyond the method itself.

Good reproducibility: value-to-distance mappings are derived in closed form per base learner (Appendix B), triangle-inequality violations of value-derived distances are quantified (Appendix D), runtime is measured in detail (Appendix I), and hyperparameters are listed per dataset (Table 14), with code and videos linked.
Hyperparameter robustness is partially addressed via a fixed-hyperparameter comparison against GAS (Table 5), where TTGS with one τ,T setting outperforms per-domain-tuned GAS on 2 of 3 domains.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: graph-based planning over replay/dataset states with subgoal feeding is well explored (SoRB, SGM, GSR, VMG, GAS, Back et al. 2025, Bagaria & Martius 2025), and the core novelty reduces to (i) applying such search purely at test time to frozen policies and (ii) a superlinear soft penalty on long edges. The contribution is best viewed as a strong engineering/re-evaluation result rather than a new idea, which some reviewers may find borderline for the main track.

Hyperparameters τ and T are tuned per dataset and base agent (Table 14 shows at least four distinct settings), which weakens the 'no tuning, plug-and-play' framing; the fixed-hyperparameter comparison with GAS helps but covers only one tuned domain.

TTGS is not uniformly beneficial: several tasks regress (e.g., HIQL antmaze-giant-navigate 65.0→63.8, antmaze-large-navigate 90.6→92.3 with some bases regressing, humanoidmaze-giant-navigate with replanning 85→78, visual-humanoidmaze near-zero everywhere), and the method is validated only on OGBench, leaving generality to other domains unverified.

Comparisons to GAS and CompDiffuser rely on numbers taken from prior papers/official repos rather than re-runs under identical conditions; setting differences are discussed but the comparison remains imperfect. The claim of being 'the first method that operates purely offline and at test time' in this category is strong and hard to verify definitively.

The soft-penalty constant (ρ(x) = x·1000^(x/τ)) and several execution details (monotonicity index, threshold T = 2τ rule) appear heuristic with limited theoretical justification; the paper compensates empirically but offers no analysis of when the shortest path on the penalized graph approximates the true optimal path.

Baseline evaluation of base learners uses default hyperparameters while TTGS adds per-task selection (the manual sweep in Appendix L includes qualitative path inspection plus random-seed-1 performance), a mild form of selection the base agents do not receive.

strengths: Comprehensive and convincing empirical evaluation: five base learners (HIQL, GCIQL, QRL, SAW, OTA) across ~27 OGBench tasks with 50 rollouts and 8 seeds, plus comparisons to GAS and CompDiffuser under a strictly more constrained setting (no training, no generative models, no online interaction).

The central empirical claim — that standard GCRL value functions encode locally consistent geometry sufficient for short-hop planning — is supported by concrete evidence: triangle-inequality violation analysis (Appendix D), value-function geometry visualizations (Appendix C), and Figure 2c showing per-step reliability degradation with horizon.

The ablations are unusually thorough for a wrapper-style method: soft vs. hard penalties (Table 10, with a clean disconnect-ratio explanation), adaptive vs. next-waypoint subgoal selection, replanning (Appendix J), clustering vs. random vertex selection (Appendix G), an L2-kNN landmark baseline (Appendix E), and a scaling sweep over graph size M (Appendix I).
The rollout-free hop-ratio diagnostic (Section 4.3) is a practical contribution, and the paper is candid that it is necessary but not sufficient, using humanoidmaze-giant-stitch as a counterexample.

Honest limitations discussion: the paper clearly states the three conditions under which TTGS helps, reports manipulation results with near-zero gains rather than hiding them, and analyzes failure modes qualitatively.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: constructing a graph over dataset states with value-derived edge costs and extracting subgoals is well-trodden territory (SoRB, SGM, SPT, VMG, GSR, GAS), all of which the related work section itself enumerates. The soft superlinear penalty and adaptive subgoal rule are sensible engineering but incremental; the paper's framing as a 're-evaluation' is a fair description of its main contribution, but that contribution is primarily empirical rather than methodological.

The 'no tuning / training-free, plug-and-play' narrative is partially undermined by the hyperparameter protocol. Table 14 shows per-dataset, per-base-learner (τ, T) settings, and Appendix L admits the pair was selected by running 1 seed and choosing the setting with the strongest task improvement — i.e., evaluation-based tuning on the very tasks being reported. The fixed-hyperparameter comparison (Table 5) partially mitigates this, but antmaze-giant-stitch drops from 78.6% to 48%, a large degradation that weakens the robustness claim.

TTGS is not uniformly beneficial: QRL+TTGS degrades on antmaze-medium-stitch (62.0→40.1) and humanoidmaze-medium-stitch (19.4→14.4), and several GCIQL and OTA cases show no gain or small regressions in Table 4. The paper's 'generally improves or maintains' framing understates this variance.

Baseline comparisons with GAS and CompDiffuser are taken from other papers/repositories under different training settings and are not run under a common protocol, so 'competitive with more complex methods' (Table 4) is suggestive rather than rigorously established.
The abstract's 'often matching or outperforming' and 'over 90%' claims rely on the best per-task tuned configurations; under the fairer fixed-hyperparameter setting the picture is more mixed.

The method assumes test-time access to dataset states and the base learner's value function — a setting restriction that is acknowledged but that limits the 'deployment' framing somewhat, and the claim to be 'the first method that operates purely offline and at test time in the offline GCRL setting' is difficult to verify and stated too strongly given, e.g., closest matches to SGM's offline graph construction.

strengths: Simple, well-motivated idea: reinterpret goal-conditioned value functions as approximate step-distance signals and use them to build a graph over the offline dataset for test-time subgoal planning. The value-to-distance mappings (Appendix B) are derived carefully per base learner, giving the method genuine plug-and-play character.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 5 base learners across the full OGBench suite (state, pixel, locomotion, manipulation; navigate/stitch/explore), 8 seeds, 50 rollouts per task, with full per-task tables. Gains are large where theory predicts (giant stitch tasks: 0-4% to 70-80%), and the paper honestly reports where TTGS does not help (manipulation, antmaze-giant-stitch with GCIQL).

Strong ablation suite that isolates each design choice: adaptive vs. next-subgoal selection, soft vs. hard edge penalty (with a disconnect-ratio analysis explaining why hard thresholds fail on stitching tasks), threshold sensitivity (Table 3), vertex-count scaling (Table 12), replanning, and clustering.

The rollout-free hop-ratio diagnostic (Section 4.3) is a nice practical addition that cleanly explains why TTGS helps in locomotion but not manipulation, and gives practitioners a pre-deployment check.

Comparison discipline: evaluates against a training-free L2-kNN landmark baseline (showing value-derived distances avoid per-environment k tuning), and against GAS under fixed cross-domain hyperparameters (Table 5), partially addressing robustness concerns. Reproducibility is excellent: runtime breakdown, hyperparameter tables, code link, and honest discussion of protocol differences when citing GAS/CompDiffuser numbers.
Limitations section is candid about dataset-access requirements, failure modes (base policy, not planner), and the conditions under which the method applies.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest. Graph/landmark planning over offline data with learned distances is well-trodden (SGM, SoRB, GSR, GAS, VMG); the core contribution is the observation that standard value functions suffice as the distance signal plus a soft edge penalty. The soft penalty itself (p(x) = x·1000/τ) is an ad hoc heuristic rather than a principled mechanism, and the paper offers no theoretical justification for why this particular form works.

Hyperparameter tuning is per-task and appears tuned on test performance. Table 14 shows per-dataset (τ, T) values for each base learner, and Appendix L admits selecting the pair that produced 'the strongest improvement in task performance' after trying 1-2 settings. This weakens the plug-and-play narrative; the fixed-hyperparameter comparison in Table 5 mitigates but does not fully eliminate this concern (that comparison covers only 7 tasks).

Headline claims of '< 1 second planning time' conflate per-episode shortest-path computation with one-time graph construction (35-100s, or ~10 minutes for pixel tasks), which is significant for practitioners deploying on new datasets.

Some comparisons rely on numbers transplanted from other papers/repositories (CompDiffuser, GAS on some tasks) under potentially differing protocols; the paper flags this but it still complicates the 'competitive with methods requiring training' claim.

Gains are inconsistent across base learners: GCIQL+TTGS shows no improvement on antmaze-giant-stitch (its local policy is unreliable), and several large-gain results have very high variance (e.g., antmaze-large-explore 26±34), suggesting the method is sensitive to base-policy competence in ways the paper acknowledges only qualitatively.
